items.readable_text:
Content:
The rules of logic provide a theory that allows us to process logical statements correctly. However, these rules do not concern themselves with the truth values of the statements involved.

Content:
Therefore, care must be taken when applying logical principles to real-world situations, as blindly following these rules does not guarantee the truthfulness of the conclusions drawn. In particular, we must also consider the truth values of the statements involved.

Content:
To demonstrate, consider the following statements:

Content:
- [MATH: P:\:] Isaac Newton was a Martian.
- [MATH: Q:\:] All Martians are from Mars.
- [MATH: R:\:] Therefore, Isaac Newton was from Mars.

Content:
Now, while statement [MATH: R] follows logically from statements [MATH: P] and [MATH: Q,] we cannot assert that [MATH: R] is true and that Isaac Newton was actually from Mars! The problem, of course, is that the statement [MATH: P] is false.

Content:
We say that a statement [MATH: \beta] follows from statements [MATH: \alpha_1, \alpha_2, \ldots, \alpha_n] if [MATH: \beta] is true whenever all of [MATH: \alpha_1, \alpha_2, \ldots, \alpha_n] are true. This is called a logical inference.

Content:
In this lesson, we'll study some well-known rules of logical inference.

items.readable_text:
Content:
The first logical inference rule we'll study is called implication elimination (or modus ponens in Latin). It states the following:

Content:
> If [MATH: P \Rightarrow Q] and [MATH: P] are both true, then [MATH: Q] must be also true.

Content:
To understand this rule, we consider the corresponding truth table:

Content:
| | | | Premise 1 | Premise 2 | Conclusion |
| [MATH: P] | [MATH: Q] | | [MATH: P \Rightarrow Q] | [MATH: P] | [MATH: Q] |
| [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm T] | | [MATH: \color{blue} \textrm T] | [MATH: \color{blue} \textrm T] | [MATH: \color{red} \textrm T] |
| [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm F] | | [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm F] |
| [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm T] | | [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm T] |
| [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm F] | | [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm F] |

Content:
Both [MATH: P \Rightarrow Q] and [MATH: P] have truth value [MATH: {\color{blue}\mathrm{T}}] (true) only in the first row of the table. For this row, [MATH: Q] is also [MATH: {\color{red}\mathrm{T}}] (true). So, according to our definition, we have a logical inference.

Content:
An alternative way of writing the rule is

Content:
[MATH: P⇒Q; P; ∴Q]

Content:
where the symbol [MATH: \,\raise{1pt}{\therefore}\,] reads as "therefore". So, the entire thing reads as follows:

Content:
> We have [MATH: P \Rightarrow Q] and [MATH: P.] Therefore, [MATH: Q.]

Content:
Since the order of the premises does not matter, we have the following variants of the rule:

Content:
[MATH: P⇒Q; P; ∴Q]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The logical inference rule of implication elimination (also known as modus ponens) asserts that if [MATH: P] implies [MATH: Q] is true, and [MATH: P] is true, then [MATH: Q] is also true.

In the case above, the modus ponens inference rule can be written as follows: [MATH: (A∧B)⇒¬C; A∧B; ∴¬C]

Therefore, the missing part is [MATH: \lnot C.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
The rules of logic provide a theory that allows us to process logical statements correctly. However, these rules do not concern themselves with the truth values of the statements involved.

Content:
Therefore, care must be taken when applying logical principles to real-world situations, as blindly following these rules does not guarantee the truthfulness of the conclusions drawn. In particular, we must also consider the truth values of the statements involved.

Content:
To demonstrate, consider the following statements:

Content:
- [MATH: P:\:] Isaac Newton was a Martian.
- [MATH: Q:\:] All Martians are from Mars.
- [MATH: R:\:] Therefore, Isaac Newton was from Mars.

Content:
Now, while statement [MATH: R] follows logically from statements [MATH: P] and [MATH: Q,] we cannot assert that [MATH: R] is true and that Isaac Newton was actually from Mars! The problem, of course, is that the statement [MATH: P] is false.

Content:
We say that a statement [MATH: \beta] follows from statements [MATH: \alpha_1, \alpha_2, \ldots, \alpha_n] if [MATH: \beta] is true whenever all of [MATH: \alpha_1, \alpha_2, \ldots, \alpha_n] are true. This is called a logical inference.

Content:
In this lesson, we'll study some well-known rules of logical inference.

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: Implication Elimination

Content:
The first logical inference rule we'll study is called implication elimination (or modus ponens in Latin). It states the following:

Content:
> If [MATH: P \Rightarrow Q] and [MATH: P] are both true, then [MATH: Q] must be also true.

Content:
To understand this rule, we consider the corresponding truth table:

Content:
| | | | Premise 1 | Premise 2 | Conclusion |
| [MATH: P] | [MATH: Q] | | [MATH: P \Rightarrow Q] | [MATH: P] | [MATH: Q] |
| [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm T] | | [MATH: \color{blue} \textrm T] | [MATH: \color{blue} \textrm T] | [MATH: \color{red} \textrm T] |
| [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm F] | | [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm F] |
| [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm T] | | [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm T] |
| [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm F] | | [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm F] |

Content:
Both [MATH: P \Rightarrow Q] and [MATH: P] have truth value [MATH: {\color{blue}\mathrm{T}}] (true) only in the first row of the table. For this row, [MATH: Q] is also [MATH: {\color{red}\mathrm{T}}] (true). So, according to our definition, we have a logical inference.

Content:
An alternative way of writing the rule is

Content:
[MATH: P⇒Q; P; ∴Q]

Content:
where the symbol [MATH: \,\raise{1pt}{\therefore}\,] reads as "therefore". So, the entire thing reads as follows:

Content:
> We have [MATH: P \Rightarrow Q] and [MATH: P.] Therefore, [MATH: Q.]

Content:
Since the order of the premises does not matter, we have the following variants of the rule:

Content:
[MATH: P⇒Q; P; ∴Q]

---

Item 3 — Tutorial: A Concrete Example

Content:
As a concrete example, let's complete the following logical inference:

Content:
[MATH: If [math]x[/math] is greater than [math]1,[/math] then [math]x[/math] is positive; [math]x[/math] is greater than [math]1[/math]; ∴A A A A A A A A A A]

Content:
The logical inference rule of implication elimination asserts that if [MATH: P] implies [MATH: Q] is true, and [MATH: P] is true, then [MATH: Q] is also true.

Content:
Let's denote:

Content:
- [MATH: P(x):] [MATH: x] is greater than [MATH: 1]
- [MATH: Q(x):] [MATH: x] is positive

Content:
Then, using the modus ponens inference rule, we obtain the following:

Content:
[MATH: P⇒Q; P; ∴Q]

Content:
Therefore, we have:

Content:
[MATH: If [math]x[/math] is greater than [math]1,[/math] then [math]x[/math] is positive; [math]x[/math] is greater than [math]1[/math]; ∴[math]x[/math] is positive]

---

Item 4 — Example: Identifying Implication Elimination

Example Prompt:

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The logical inference rule of implication elimination (also known as modus ponens) asserts that if [MATH: P] implies [MATH: Q] is true, and [MATH: P] is true, then [MATH: Q] is also true.

In the case above, the modus ponens inference rule can be written as follows:
[MATH: (A∧B)⇒¬C; A∧B; ∴¬C]

Therefore, the missing part is [MATH: \lnot C.]

Item 10 — Tutorial: Denying the Consequent

Content:
Let's now consider another logical inference rule called denying the consequent (or modus tollens in Latin):

Content:
[MATH: P⇒Q; ¬Q; ∴¬P]

Content:
It reads as follows:

Content:
> We have [MATH: P \Rightarrow Q] and [MATH: \lnot Q.] Therefore, [MATH: \lnot P.]

Content:
We can use a truth table to check that the rule is valid.

Content:
| | | | Premise 1 | Premise 2 | Conclusion |
| [MATH: P] | [MATH: Q] | | [MATH: P \Rightarrow Q] | [MATH: \lnot Q] | [MATH: \lnot P] |
| [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm T] | | [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm F] |
| [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm F] | | [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm F] |
| [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm T] | | [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm T] |
| [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm F] | | [MATH: \color{blue} \textrm T] | [MATH: \color{blue} \textrm T] | [MATH: \color{red} \textrm T] |

Content:
Both [MATH: P \Rightarrow Q] and [MATH: \lnot Q] have the truth value [MATH: {\color{blue}\mathrm{T}}] (true) only in the fourth row of the table. For this row, [MATH: \lnot P] also has truth value [MATH: {\color{red}\mathrm{T}}] (true). So, according to the definition, we have a logical inference.

Content:
Since the order of the premises does not matter, we have the following variants of the rule:

Content:
[MATH: P⇒Q; ¬Q; ∴¬P]
